title: JESUS WASHED THEIR FEET. SO WHY DO SOME CHURCH LEADERS EXPECT EVERYONE TO KISS THEIRS?
paragraphs: JESUS WASHED THEIR FEET. SO WHY DO SOME CHURCH LEADERS EXPECT EVERYONE TO KISS THEIRS?

The night Jesus knelt before His disciples, He exposed a kind of spiritual pride that still hides behind pulpits, titles, expensive suits, and the demand to be treated like royalty. And the most uncomfortable question isn't just what some pastors have become. It's whether we've forgotten what Christian leadership was supposed to look like.
Imagine walking into a church where the pastor is treated like a king.

People rush to carry his belongings. Someone makes sure his preferred seat is waiting. Others are expected to stand when he enters. His opinions are rarely questioned. His decisions are treated as though they came directly from heaven.
A struggling widow might wait weeks for pastoral care.
But the leader's comfort? That must be attended to immediately.
A wounded church member might be told to remain silent for the sake of unity.
But a perceived insult against the pastor? That demands an apology.
And somewhere in the middle of all this, the congregation is reminded to be humble, to sacrifice, to serve, and to become more like Jesus.
Something is terribly wrong with that picture.
Not because pastors shouldn't be respected.
Not because ministry leaders don't deserve encouragement, appropriate financial support, rest, or genuine appreciation.
Scripture teaches that they do.
But because the moment Christian leadership becomes more concerned with being served than serving, it begins to contradict the very Lord whose name it claims to represent.
And the most disturbing part?
Jesus already confronted this problem.
Not from a magnificent throne.
Not from a platform surrounded by admirers.
Not with a speech demanding recognition.
He confronted it with a towel.
And a basin of water.
And the dirty feet of men who still didn't fully understand Him.
THE NIGHT THE KING GOT ON HIS KNEES
It was the night before the crucifixion.
The shadow of betrayal was already falling across the upper room. Judas was preparing to betray Him. Peter would soon deny Him. The others would scatter when danger arrived.
Jesus knew what was coming.
He knew the Father had given all things into His hands. He knew He had come from God and was returning to God.
John records this extraordinary moment in John 13:3–5.
And what did Jesus do with that knowledge of His authority?
He rose from supper.
He laid aside His outer garments.
He took a towel.
He wrapped it around Himself.
Then He poured water into a basin and began washing His disciples' feet.
Read that slowly.
The One who possessed all authority chose to perform the work of a servant.
The hands that would soon be pierced by nails were washing dust from human feet.
The One whom angels worship was kneeling before imperfect men.
The Lord of glory was doing something many people considered too lowly for someone of importance.
And He wasn't pretending to be humble.
He was revealing what divine greatness looks like when it enters a room full of human pride.

In the first-century world, feet became dirty from walking along dusty roads in sandals. Footwashing was a familiar act of hospitality, often performed by servants or those occupying a lowly position.
Jesus deliberately assumed that lowly role.
And here is the detail we cannot afford to miss.
Jesus did not wash their feet because He had forgotten who He was. He washed their feet precisely because He knew who He was.
His humility did not come from insecurity.
It came from perfect love.
Some leaders today seem terrified that serving ordinary people will diminish their authority.
Jesus demonstrated that true authority has nothing to fear from humility.
Peter was horrified.
"Lord, dost thou wash my feet?" (John 13:6, KJV).
He couldn't understand why the Master would kneel before the disciple.
Jesus answered that Peter did not yet understand what He was doing, but would understand afterward.
When Peter refused, Jesus told him, "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me" (John 13:8, KJV).
This was more than a lesson in good manners.
It pointed to our need to receive cleansing from Christ. Before we can imitate the Servant, we must first receive what only the Savior can give.
We do not wash our way into salvation through good deeds.
We are cleansed by the grace of Jesus Christ.
And the One who cleanses us calls us to become servants of others.
After washing their feet, Jesus returned to His place and asked a question that should still trouble every person entrusted with spiritual authority.
"Know ye what I have done to you?" (John 13:12, KJV).
Then He said:
"If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." (John 13:14, KJV).
Notice what He didn't say.
He didn't say, "Now that you've seen Me humble Myself, make sure everyone honors your position."
He didn't say, "The higher your calling, the less ordinary service you should perform."
He didn't say, "When people recognize your anointing, they should protect you from inconvenient people."
He said they ought to wash one another's feet.
And in John 13:15, He explained:
"For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you."
This was not merely a beautiful moment for a painting.
It was a command that challenged their understanding of greatness.
And it still challenges ours.
THE GREEK WORD THAT EXPOSES OUR OBSESSION WITH STATUS
To understand how radically Jesus challenged the world's idea of leadership, we need to listen carefully to His words elsewhere in the Gospels.
In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus confronted the disciples' ambition for prominence.
He observed that those regarded as rulers among the Gentiles exercised authority over others in domineering ways.
Then He declared:
"But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister." (Mark 10:43, KJV).
The Greek word translated "minister" is διάκονος (diakonos).
It refers to a servant, attendant, or one who ministers to others.
Jesus continued by saying that whoever wanted to be first must become the servant of all.
In Mark 10:44, the word translated "servant" is δοῦλος (doulos), a word commonly referring to a slave or bondservant.
These are not words associated with personal grandeur.
They communicate service, humility, and a willingness to put others before oneself.
And then Jesus gave the reason.
"For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." (Mark 10:45, KJV).
The Greek verb behind "to minister" is related to diakonos.
The point is unmistakable.
Jesus did not come to build a comfortable empire around Himself.
He came to serve.
Ultimately, He gave His life as a ransom for many.
His death was not merely an example of generosity. It was His unique, saving sacrifice for sinners.
No pastor can repeat that redemptive work.
But every pastor is called to follow the humility of the Savior who accomplished it.
Now consider the implications.
If the sinless Son of God came not to be served but to serve, what biblical argument allows a sinful human leader to make personal privilege the defining feature of ministry?
What kind of discipleship teaches people to imitate Christ's humility while excusing their leader from practicing it?
And how did we become so impressed by the appearance of spiritual power that we sometimes overlook the absence of Christlike character?
These are not questions meant to destroy the church.
They are questions meant to call the church back to Jesus.
WHEN HONOR BECOMES SOMETHING DANGEROUS
There is nothing inherently sinful about honoring a pastor.
First Timothy 5:17 speaks of elders who rule well being worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching.
First Timothy 5:18 supports the principle that a worker deserves appropriate compensation.
First Thessalonians 5:12–13 calls believers to recognize and esteem those who labor among them and care for them in the Lord.
Hebrews 13:17 teaches believers to respect and respond appropriately to faithful spiritual oversight, reminding us that leaders must give an account.
Scripture does not endorse contempt for pastoral leadership.
But neither does it give pastors unlimited authority.
Honor is not worship.
Respect is not unquestioning submission.
Generosity is not permission for financial exploitation.
Unity is not the silencing of legitimate concerns.
And spiritual accountability is not rebellion.
In fact, Scripture gives us clear instructions for handling accusations against elders.
First Timothy 5:19–20 requires proper evidence before receiving an accusation and calls for public rebuke when an elder persists in sin.
These protections matter in both directions.
Leaders should not be destroyed by unsupported allegations.
And members should not be intimidated into silence when credible wrongdoing needs to be addressed.
The biblical standard is neither a culture of suspicion nor a culture of untouchable leaders.
It is truth, justice, holiness, and accountability before God.
Consider 1 Peter 5:2–3.
Peter instructed elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for dishonest gain, and not as those who lord it over the people entrusted to them, but as examples to the flock.
The Greek expression κατακυριεύοντες (katakyrieuontes) conveys the idea of exercising mastery or domineering authority over others.
Peter specifically forbids that attitude in shepherding.
And Peter understood the lesson personally.
He was there when Jesus washed his feet.
The man who once resisted being served by a kneeling Messiah later warned church elders not to dominate God's people.
That is not a coincidence we should ignore.
It is a transformation worth remembering.
THE PEOPLE JESUS NEVER ASKED US TO OVERLOOK
Think about the single mother who has barely enough money to feed her children.
She comes to church exhausted.
She wants prayer.
She needs someone to remind her that God sees her.
But suppose she encounters a culture where the leader's image receives more attention than the congregation's suffering.
Where people are celebrated for their financial contributions but quietly overlooked when they can no longer give.
Where questions about money are dismissed as attacks against God's anointed.
Where ordinary members are expected to sacrifice without being shown the same compassion.
Something deeply biblical has been lost.
Not every large church operates this way.
Not every pastor with a salary, a vehicle, a security team, or a comfortable home is guilty of greed.
The size of a ministry or the possessions of a leader do not, by themselves, establish sin.
Circumstances, responsibilities, safety, stewardship, and transparency matter.
We must never confuse simplicity with automatic holiness or prosperity with automatic corruption.
But we must also never confuse outward success with God's approval.
Jesus told us to examine fruit.
Character matters.
Truth matters.
How vulnerable people are treated matters.
Financial integrity matters.
The willingness to be corrected matters.
And the way a leader behaves when nobody important is watching may reveal more about their heart than an hour behind a pulpit.
A shepherd is not called to feed on the sheep.
A shepherd is called to care for them.
In Ezekiel 34, the Lord condemned shepherds of Israel who cared for themselves while neglecting the flock.
The weak were not strengthened.
The sick were not healed.
The injured were not bound up.
The lost were not sought.
Instead, harshness and force characterized their rule.
The immediate context concerns Israel's unfaithful shepherds, but the passage reveals a lasting truth about God's character: He opposes leaders who exploit those entrusted to their care.
And in Ezekiel 34:23, God promises a shepherd from the line of David.
That promise ultimately directs our attention to Jesus Christ, the Good Shepherd.
He is the answer to failed shepherding.
He does not merely expose corrupt leadership.
He shows us the perfect Shepherd.
AND THEN THERE WAS JUDAS
There is another detail in John 13 that makes the scene even more astonishing.
Judas was present.
John tells us that Jesus already knew who would betray Him.
Yet the account describes Jesus washing the disciples' feet without recording an exception for Judas.
The natural reading is that Judas was included, though John does not separately narrate the washing of his feet.
Think about the weight of that moment.
Jesus knew betrayal was approaching.
He knew one of the men at the table would hand Him over.
And still, He took the posture of a servant.
This does not mean Jesus approved of Judas's betrayal.
He did not.
Love does not require pretending that evil is good.
But it reveals something breathtaking about Christ's humility.
He was not serving because the disciples had earned it.
He was serving because His love was greater than their worthiness.
Now bring that truth into the church today.
If Jesus could stoop so low before men who would fail Him, how can any spiritual leader justify treating struggling believers as beneath their dignity?
How can someone preach grace while showing contempt toward the broken?
How can someone speak of forgiveness while using shame to control the congregation?
How can someone proclaim the cross while building a ministry culture centered on personal superiority?
A ministry may have excellent music.
A beautiful building.
A powerful online presence.
Thousands of followers.
And still need to return to the basin.
Because the evidence of Christlike leadership is not merely how many people listen when you speak.
It is also how faithfully you love when serving costs you something.
BUT BEFORE WE POINT AT THE PULPIT, WE NEED TO LOOK IN THE MIRROR
This is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because pride is not confined to pastors.
Some of us criticize leaders for wanting special treatment while becoming furious when our own contributions go unnoticed.
We serve until someone forgets to thank us.
We give until someone else receives recognition.
We volunteer until our preferences are challenged.
We say we want to glorify God, but secretly hope people will notice how much we are doing for Him.
And when nobody notices?
Our hearts begin keeping score.
Perhaps you have served in a ministry for years.
You arrived early.
You stayed late.
You prayed for people who never knew your name.
Then someone newer received the position you wanted.
And suddenly, the joy disappeared.
Maybe the problem wasn't only that you were tired.
Maybe part of your heart had begun to crave the very recognition Jesus taught us not to worship.
I know this is difficult to confront.
But the Gospel doesn't expose our pride to humiliate us.
It exposes what needs to be surrendered so that grace can transform us.
Philippians 2:3–5 calls believers to reject selfish ambition and vain glory, to consider others, and to have the mind of Christ.
Then Paul directs our eyes to Jesus.
Though He existed in the form of God, He did not treat His equality with God as something to exploit for His own advantage.
Instead, He took the form of a servant.
He humbled Himself.
He became obedient unto death.
Even death on a cross.
The Greek word ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen) in Philippians 2:7 is commonly translated "made himself of no reputation" in the KJV, or "emptied himself" in many modern translations.
It does not mean Jesus stopped being God or surrendered His divine nature.
The passage explains His self-humbling through His taking the form of a servant and entering genuine human life.
The eternal Son did not cease to be divine.
He willingly embraced the lowliness of human servanthood.
And His humility carried Him all the way to Calvary.
The basin was not the end of the story.
The cross was coming.
THE SCANDAL WAS NOT THAT JESUS KNELT. THE SCANDAL WAS THAT OUR PRIDE MADE HIS SACRIFICE NECESSARY.
We often speak about the scandal of corrupt leadership.
And rightly so when spiritual authority is abused.
But Scripture reveals a deeper scandal.
The human heart is so infected by sin that we can turn even the things of God into instruments of self-exaltation.
We can use ministry to build a name for ourselves.
We can use theological knowledge to look down on others.
We can use generosity to purchase admiration.
We can use religious language to hide selfish motives.
We can even use the appearance of humility to become proud of how humble we seem.
Sin is not always loud.
Sometimes it wears a suit.
Sometimes it carries a Bible.
Sometimes it stands behind a pulpit.
And sometimes it sits quietly in the congregation, judging everyone else while refusing to repent.
That is why the answer cannot simply be better public relations, stricter church etiquette, or a new generation of more charismatic leaders.
We need more than improved religious behavior.
We need Jesus.
We need His forgiveness.
His truth.
His cleansing.
His transforming grace.
We need to remember that no human pastor is the head of the church.
Christ is the Head of the church. (Colossians 1:18).
No spiritual leader can replace the Mediator between God and humanity.
There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. (1 Timothy 2:5).
No title can elevate a person beyond the need for repentance.
No ministry accomplishment can erase the requirement for integrity.
And no amount of public admiration can substitute for a heart surrendered to Christ.
WHAT ABOUT THE PASTORS WHO ARE QUIETLY GETTING IT RIGHT?
We must speak about them too.
Because there are faithful shepherds who will never become famous.
Pastors who visit hospital rooms after exhausting days.
Pastors who pray with grieving families when cameras are nowhere to be found.
Pastors who preach faithfully to small congregations, even when the offering barely covers the bills.
Pastors who admit when they are wrong.
Who welcome appropriate accountability.
Who protect children and vulnerable people.
Who refuse to manipulate generosity.
Who care more about the spiritual health of their people than the size of their platform.
Some are exhausted.
Some are underpaid.
Some carry burdens their congregations will never fully understand.
And they deserve our prayers, respect, encouragement, and practical support.
The answer to abusive leadership is not to despise all leadership.
It is to recover biblical leadership.
The church needs faithful pastors.
Not celebrities who cannot be questioned.
Not spiritual performers who need constant applause.
Not frightened leaders who avoid every difficult truth.
But shepherds who love Christ, teach His Word, protect His flock, and remember that they themselves belong to the Chief Shepherd.
And congregations must do their part.
A church should not demand endless sacrifice from its pastor while refusing to provide reasonable care, rest, compensation, and accountability.
Servant leadership is not permission for a congregation to exploit its shepherd.
The same Jesus who washed feet also taught that the laborer is worthy of his hire (Luke 10:7).
Biblical humility does not abolish responsibility, boundaries, or healthy support.
It puts love and faithfulness at the center of them.
THE TOWEL IS STILL WAITING
Imagine what could change if churches truly returned to John 13.
Imagine pastors who could be approached without fear.
Church members who could ask sincere questions without automatically being accused of rebellion.
Financial decisions handled with integrity and appropriate transparency.
Leaders who listen before defending themselves.
Members who honor faithful shepherds without idolizing them.
People who serve without turning their sacrifice into a competition.
Churches where the wounded are protected, the poor are remembered, the truth is preached, and repentance is practiced by everyone.
Not a perfect church.
There is no perfect congregation on this side of eternity.
But a repentant church.
A teachable church.
A church where the authority of Scripture is greater than the personality of any leader.
A church that remembers why it exists.
Not to build monuments to human greatness.
But to proclaim the excellencies of the One who called us out of darkness into His marvelous light (1 Peter 2:9).
And perhaps that restoration begins with a question far more personal than, "Why won't my pastor wash feet?"
Perhaps it begins with:
"Lord, whose feet have I been unwilling to wash?"
The person who offended you?
The family member who disappointed you?
The struggling believer you quietly judged?
The ministry volunteer whose work you took for granted?
The person who cannot offer you anything in return?
Jesus never told us that serving would always feel rewarding.
He told us to follow Him.
And sometimes following Him means choosing the towel when our flesh desperately wants the throne.
IF THIS EXPOSED SOMETHING IN YOU, DON'T RUN FROM IT
Maybe you're a pastor reading this, and you recognize that the demands of ministry have slowly hardened your heart.
You began wanting to help people.
But somewhere along the way, criticism became unbearable, recognition became addictive, and control began to feel like security.
There is still grace for repentance.
You do not have to protect a false image of yourself.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek accountability.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Repair what can be repaired.
And remember that genuine repentance includes changed behavior, not merely emotional apologies.
Perhaps you're a church member who has been wounded by spiritual manipulation.
You were told that asking questions meant you lacked faith.
You were pressured to give what you couldn't afford.
You were made to feel that protecting a leader's reputation mattered more than telling the truth.
Please hear this carefully.
Jesus is not the author of that manipulation.
Your worth before God is not determined by your usefulness to a ministry.
And honoring spiritual leadership does not require accepting abuse.
Seek wise, trustworthy support. Where wrongdoing has occurred, pursue appropriate protection and accountability.
You can love Christ without defending everything done in His name.
And perhaps you're simply tired.
Tired of church politics.
Tired of religious performances.
Tired of seeing people wounded by those who were supposed to care for them.
Before you give up on Jesus because of the failures of people who claim to represent Him, look again at the upper room.
Look at the towel.
Look at the basin.
Look at the Savior kneeling.
Then follow Him to the cross.
The One who gave His life for you is not the same as every person who has misused His name.
Jesus remains faithful even when human leaders fail.
And His invitation still stands.
Come to Him.
Not because you have earned His love.
But because He is merciful.
Not because you can clean yourself up first.
But because He is the Savior who cleanses sinners.
Not because your past is spotless.
But because His grace is greater than your sin.
First John 1:9 assures believers that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
That promise is not permission to continue in sin without repentance.
It is hope for those who turn toward the God who forgives.
This is the heart of our message at Gospel Warrior.
Not because Jesus pretends that sin never happened.
Not because grace makes consequences disappear.
But because through His death and resurrection, He offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the power of a transformed life.
The scandal of our pride does not have to be the final chapter.
The disgrace of our failures does not have to become our eternal identity.
In Christ, repentance can lead to restoration.
And broken people can become living testimonies of mercy.
NOW THE QUESTION IS WHAT WE WILL DO WITH WHAT WE HAVE READ
Some messages are meant to comfort us.
Others are meant to confront us.
This one may need to do both.
If you are a church leader, ask yourself whether the people entrusted to you experience the tenderness and truth of Christ through your leadership.
If you are a church member, ask whether you are encouraging faithful leadership while refusing to make an idol of any human being.
And if you are someone still healing from a painful church experience, remember that your story does not have to end where someone else failed you.
Jesus is still worthy of your trust.
If this message stirred something you have been afraid to admit, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not have to disclose painful details publicly to be heard or cared for.
Perhaps someone reading your words will realize they are not alone.
Perhaps someone will stop defending an unhealthy pattern.
Perhaps a leader will be moved toward repentance.
Perhaps a wounded believer will find the courage to seek help.
And perhaps someone who has been far from Christ will begin to see His beauty again.
Not to shame the church.
Not to stir up hatred toward pastors.
But to remind people that Christian leadership must always be measured by the character and teaching of Jesus Christ.
A single thoughtful share may reach someone who has never heard the difference between biblical authority and spiritual domination.
Return to John 13 when pride starts whispering that you deserve more recognition.
Return to Mark 10 when leadership begins to look more like privilege than service.
Return to Philippians 2 when you need to remember the mind of Christ.
Invite your family, your friends, your pastor, your ministry team, the believer who is growing weary, and even the seeker who is still asking questions about Jesus.

We want this community to be a place where people are not merely inspired for a moment, but encouraged to open their Bibles, examine their hearts, repent where necessary, and grow in the grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ.
AND IF YOU WANT TO HELP THIS MINISTRY KEEP SERVING, THERE IS A WAY TO STAND WITH US
At Gospel Warrior, we believe that the truth of Scripture should continue reaching people who are hurting, searching, questioning, repenting, and learning to walk with Christ.
That is why we continue creating Gospel-centered articles, biblical encouragement, discipleship materials, and resources designed to point people toward Jesus rather than toward human personalities.
These resources are part of our commitment to making biblical nourishment accessible.
But producing, maintaining, and expanding ministry resources also takes time, work, and financial support.
It is a voluntary act of partnership in the ongoing work of this ministry.
And nobody should feel pressured to give money they need for basic necessities.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come from the heart, not from compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the kind of support we want.
Not guilt.
Not manipulation.
Not promises that money will purchase divine favor.
But willing partnership, grounded in gratitude to God and love for people.
It is the opportunity to help keep Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to people who need them.
You can pray for this ministry.
You can encourage someone with Scripture.
You can help another believer take one more step toward Jesus.
That matters.
Because the mission is not to build an audience that admires Gospel Warrior.
The mission is to point people toward the Savior who deserves all glory.
ONE LAST THING BEFORE YOU GO
When Jesus finished washing His disciples' feet, He did not ask them to build a monument to the moment.
He asked them to follow His example.
In John 13:17, He said:
"If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them." (KJV).
Notice that last phrase.
If ye do them.
Not merely if you preach them.
Not if you post them.
Not if you agree with them.
Not if you applaud someone else for saying them.
If you do them.
The real test of this article is not whether it makes us angry at proud leaders.
It is whether it makes us more willing to serve like Jesus.
Because one day, every earthly title will lose its importance.
Every platform will fall silent.
Every human reputation will stand beneath the perfect judgment of God.
And what will matter is not how many people bowed before us.
It will be whether we truly belonged to Jesus Christ, trusted in His saving grace, and followed Him in faithful obedience.
The church does not need more people competing for the highest seat.
It needs people who remember the Savior who took the lowest place.
So pastor, love your people.
Church member, honor faithful shepherds.
Wounded believer, keep your eyes on Christ.
And to every one of us who has ever secretly wanted the throne:
Remember the towel.
Remember the basin.
Remember the cross.
The hands that washed their feet were the same hands that would be nailed to a cross for their sins—and He never once needed a throne made of human applause to prove He was King.
